I'd be lying if I said I understand how, but as far as I understand, the paper claims to have proven P =/= NP by proving that any program that solves an NP problem is too complex to be reduced to a program that runs in polynomial time.

Background on P and NP:

Problems in computing are organized by how difficult they are to solve. The typical way to measure this is by how the problem scales. For example, summing two numbers is easy, and doesn't get significantly harder if you're asked to sum three or four. This is a P problem, the complexity scales polynomialy, meaning the time it takes doesn't grow faster than N^a, where N is the amount of numbers to sum and a is a power.

NP is the class of all problems of which the solution can be checked in polynomial time. So all P problems are also NP: to check the solution, just solve again. But there are also NP problems that seem a lot harder. For example, give me 20 distinct prime numbers that sum to 2543. That's a very difficult task to solve. However, given such a list, it's easy to check if the answer is correct, just sum those twenty numbers.

It's assumed no algorithm exists that can "easily" solve these NP problems, that there is no P solution for some NP problems, meaning that NP =/= P. But (up until now, maybe?) no one has been able to prove it.

Expanding on this (and bastardising what I have picked up elsewhere), the proof considers one type of NP-hard problem, the Clique Decision Problem. This problem has been proven to be NP-complete, that is, a solution for this problem can be turned into a solution for any NP problem.

The proof then uses Boolean networks without the NOT function (monotone Boolean networks) to solve the Clique Decision problem. He then uses these to produce an approximaiton to the lower bound for the complexity of solving the Clique Decision Problem, and shows that this must be exponential. This is then extended to general Boolean networks (i.e. not necesserily monotone) with an argument that introducing NOT gates can not reduce the complexity to polynomial. Hence the Clique Decision Problem has no polynomial solution and P != NP.

There have been other proofs that have shown that this type of technique can only be used to prove a quadratic lower bound. However, the author references another paper of his own that states that relaxing one of the conditions of the quadratic lower bound proof can lead to super polynomial lower bounds.

The author is an active researcher in this field and not just some crackpot. Some people have commented that the maths in this paper does not seem strong/novel enough to solve the P ?= NP problem, and expect that a flaw will be found. Whether that is the case, and whether the flaw will lead to an interesting advance in the field remains to be seen.
